abstract: Development accounting is a simple tool with potentially powerful insights. It asks whether the measured differences in inputs between developing and developed countries can account for the gap in GDP per worker. Twenty years ago, Francesco Caselli famously argued that the best estimate was “no”. This column revisits that conclusion in light of two decades of intensive research. The authors show that inputs account for a much higher share than previously thought – between 55% and 70%, as opposed to 30% before. An expanded measure of human capital that incorporates education quality and work experience drives much of this result.
title: Accounting for cross-country income differences: Two decades of progress

abstract: Tokenised finance has moved from the margins of crypto markets to the centre of the policy agenda. Central banks, regulators, and market participants are debating how far it could reshape the issuance, trading, and settlement of securities, including what this would mean for financial markets and monetary policy. This column argues that while tokenisation offers considerable promise — including near-instant settlement, round-the-clock operations, and higher velocity of liquidity and collateral — the transition to a tokenised world will not be frictionless. The coexistence of 24/7 on-chain systems with traditional off-chain infrastructures could create new challenges for market functioning and monetary policy implementation.
title: Tokenised finance: Towards better markets?

abstract: In response to digital dependence, Europe has decided to think bigger. This includes AI gigafactories, tripling data centre capacity, and searching for domestic champions. However, this column argues that the destination for 2050 should be different. For the first time since the railway age, small, open AI models that run close to the data are making it possible for network technologies to distribute economic power rather than concentrate it. Europe’s dense network of small firms, regions, and languages puts it in a strong position to reap the benefits, provided today’s rules on switching, procurement, computing, and diffusion are designed with a mesh in mind rather than a hub.
title: Small is beautiful 2050: Europe’s digital economy as a mesh, not a hub
